intro.title: Explore Guachimontones
intro.description: The Zona Arqueológica Teuchitlán o Guachimontones is located in the municipality of Teuchitlán, Jalisco, Mexico. It is a unique archaeological site famous for its stunning pre-Hispanic circular pyramids. This site represents one of the most notable examples of pre-Columbian circular architecture in Mesoamerica, offering visitors a fascinating window into the ancient Teuchitlán culture.

visitGuide.title: Visiting Tips
items: The site is open to the public, verify opening hours before visiting
Hire a local guide for detailed information about the site's history
Bring hat, sunscreen, and water as there is little shade
Visit the site museum to see archaeological artifacts and models

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: Circular pyramids: One of the extremely rare circular stepped pyramid complexes in Mesoamerica, showcasing the unique architectural features of the Teuchitlán culture.
Cultural heritage: An archaeological site officially recognized and protected by INAH (National Institute of Anthropology and History).
Living history: Explore ruins of an ancient civilization dating back to 300 BCE (Late Preclassic period).
Prime location: Located in Jalisco state, easily accessible from Guadalajara.

intro.equivalence: The Zona Arqueológica Teuchitlán o Guachimontones, widely known as Guachimontones, lies in the heart of Teuchitlan, Jalisco, Mexico, and is a great starting point for exploring western Jalisco.

surroundings.text: When visiting the Zona Arqueológica Teuchitlán o Guachimontones, visitors can easily round out the day by exploring nearby landmarks and points of interest such as the Pueblo Magico of Tequila and Laguna de La Vega.

Laguna de La Vega: a natural recreation area a few minutes from Teuchitlan, ideal for relaxing by the water.
Teuchitlan town center: church, plazas and local food for a meal after your archaeological visit.

sections.title: Historical Significance
sections.content: Guachimontones is an archaeological site of the Teuchitlán culture, which flourished between 200 BCE and 400 CE. The site is famous for its distinctive circular structures, including circular pyramids with altars at the top, circular plazas, and ball courts.

sections.title: Archaeological Landscape
sections.content: The site is located in a beautiful natural setting with views of the Sierra de Tequila. The circular structures are surrounded by typical vegetation of Jalisco, creating a unique atmosphere where history and nature meet.

sections.title: Visiting Experience
sections.content: Visiting Guachimontones is a fascinating experience. You can walk among the ancient circular pyramids, learn about the Teuchitlán culture at the site museum, and enjoy the stunning views of the surrounding landscape.

items.q: What are the circular pyramids of Guachimontones?
items.a: They are ceremonial structures with a circular ground plan built by the Teuchitlán culture. Unlike the rectangular Maya or Aztec pyramids, the stepped temples here form concentric circles around a central altar - a design almost unique in Mesoamerica.

items.q: Where is Guachimontones and how do I get there from Guadalajara?
items.a: The site lies in the municipality of Teuchitlán, Jalisco, about 75 km (46 mi) west of Guadalajara, roughly a 1.5-hour drive. You can reach it by private car, by bus from Guadalajara's bus station to Teuchitlán, or on an organized tour from the city.

items.q: How much does the entrance cost and what are the opening hours?
items.a: Admission is ticketed and the usual opening hours are Thursday to Sunday, 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; the site is closed from Monday to Wednesday. Prices and discounts may change, so we recommend confirming by phone before your visit.

items.q: Can you climb the main pyramid?
items.a: No. Climbing is strictly forbidden to protect the archaeological structures. Viewpoints and marked trails let you appreciate them up close.

items.q: How much time do I need to visit Guachimontones?
items.a: Allow 2 to 3 hours to comfortably explore the site and its museum. If you also plan to eat in Teuchitlán or combine the visit with a nearby town, set aside a full half day.

items.q: What facilities are available at the site?
items.a: The archaeological zone has parking, restrooms and a site museum included in the visit. Facilities are basic: bring water, a hat and comfortable shoes, as most of the route is outdoors with little shade.

items.q: Is Guachimontones suitable for a visit with children?
items.a: Yes. The site museum and the walking trails are very educational for children. The terrain is uneven and shade is limited, so bring water, a hat, sunscreen and closed shoes for the whole family.

items.q: What is the best time of year to visit Guachimontones?
items.a: The dry season, from November to April, is the most comfortable time to explore the site. During the rainy season (June-October) the landscape is greener, but check the weather forecast before you go.

guideHistory.metaTitle: History of Guachimontones' Circular Pyramids & the Teuchitlán Culture
guideHistory.metaDescription: The Teuchitlán tradition built circular pyramids unique in Mesoamerica: learn about their history, circular architecture and meaning.
guideHistory.h1: History of the Circular Pyramids & the Teuchitlán Culture
guideHistory.lede: Guachimontones is the best-known achievement of the Teuchitlán tradition, a little-known culture that developed a circular ceremonial architecture without parallel in Mesoamerica.

blocks.h: Why are the pyramids of Guachimontones circular?
blocks.p: While most Mesoamerican cultures built pyramids with a rectangular base, the people of the Teuchitlán tradition raised stepped circular platforms around circular plazas, with an altar in the middle. The ensemble, known as a guachimontón, appears to be linked to community ceremonies, agricultural cycles and the worship of nature forces in western Mexico.
items: Signature structure: the guachimontón, a stepped pyramid with a circular ground plan
The compounds combine concentric circles, circular plazas and ball courts
It is a development of western Mexico, not a Maya or Aztec influence

blocks.h: The Teuchitlán tradition: who built it
blocks.p: Between 300 BCE and 400 CE, the Teuchitlán river basin was the centre of an agricultural society organised around lakes and volcanic lands. Its pottery and settlements reveal a complex culture with long-distance exchange, recognised by archaeologists as one of the most original developments of ancient Mexico.
items: Peak period: Late Preclassic to Classic (c. 300 BCE - 400 CE)
Economic base: farming, fishing and regional trade
Linked to the shaft tombs typical of western Mexico

blocks.p: Researchers formally documented the site from the 1970s onwards, and INAH has explored and preserved it since the 1990s. Today its structures are open to the public and it has a site museum.
items: Ceremonial core with the Main Pyramid as its largest structure
Dozens of related structures and compounds in the Teuchitlán valley
Excavation and restoration carried out by INAH
The site museum displays pieces and explains the life of the Teuchitlán tradition

blocks.p: Unlike Maya or Central-Mexican centres, which were organised around rectangular plazas and pyramids, Guachimontones orders its space in circles. It also lacks monumental stelae or hieroglyphic writing: its grandeur lies in circular geometry and the scale of its ceremonial compounds.
items: Maya and Aztec: rectangular or stepped temple bases
Teotihuacan: great platforms aligned along a causeway
Guachimontones: concentric circles, a central altar and round plazas

blocks.h: Deep origins in the valley (from c. 1000 BCE)
blocks.p: INAH describes Guachimontones as the first great population centre of western Mexico. Its earliest phase, marked by shaft tombs in the El Opeño style, developed alongside other Mesoamerican societies before the ceremonial circles took their classic form.
items: Beginnings around 1000 BCE in the lake-and-volcano highlands of Jalisco
A dispersed pattern of settlements arranged around a ceremonial core, rather than a single dense city
The tradition's end is linked to the arrival of new western cultural horizons, such as metallurgy and the bow and arrow

blocks.p: Officially the zone is known as Guachimontones or Teuchitlán, the second name shared with the nearby town. Around the site, oral tradition keeps the ancient landscape alive: visitors may hear different versions of local stories from guides or in the town, best understood as living heritage rather than scientific record.
items: Two official names coexist: the archaeological zone and the nearby municipality
Guides and museum staff can share the best-grounded stories told in the region
Local tales connect the round mounds, the volcano and the lake with the pre-Hispanic past

facilities.title: Visitor Services & Nearby Amenities
facilities.subtitle: A neutral, type-level overview — we do not advertise specific businesses. Services and their opening days change often; always confirm on site or in town.

items.d: Toilets are usually available near the entrance or visitor area. Carry your own tissue and hand gel — availability can vary.
There is a parking area by the entrance (the surface is sometimes unpaved). Free parking or a small fee may apply depending on the season.
Entrance staff and official guides can help with practical questions. Ask about a guided visit for deeper context on the site.
Food, pets and smoking are generally not allowed inside the zone. Keep snacks and meals for outside and leave a water bottle in your vehicle.
The town offers casual local options: family-run eateries, taco stands and small cafés serving regional Jalisco food. Opening days are fewer midweek.
Small markets, bakeries and convenience stores in town cover water, snacks and basic supplies. For larger supermarkets, head to the bigger towns on the highway.
Modest hotels, guesthouses and rural cabins are available in the area, with more choice in nearby Tala or Guadalajara. Weekends fill up quickly — book ahead.
Fuel stations are found along the main approach roads and in larger towns. Electric-vehicle charging is scarce near the site, so charge before leaving the city.
ATMs are limited — carry cash. A pharmacy is usually available in town. For emergencies dial 911 and head to the nearest larger town or Guadalajara.

facilities.note: All the points above describe typical availability and service types only — not specific businesses.

seasons.title: When to Visit: a Seasonal Guide
seasons.subtitle: Guachimontones sits in Jalisco's temperate highlands (around 1,300 m). The climate follows a clear dry season and a rainy season — here is how the year usually looks.

rows.weather: Clear skies, mild sunny days and cool nights; almost no rain.
rows.highlights: The most comfortable months for walking the site and taking photographs; the views stay open.
rows.tips: Bring a light jacket for the early hours. Weekends can be busier.

rows.weather: The driest and hottest weeks; strong sun and daytime temperatures near 30 °C.
rows.highlights: Crisp light for photographing the circular structures against the valley.
rows.tips: Arrive at opening time, keep to the shade and drink water throughout the day.

rows.weather: Warm and humid; most rain arrives as afternoon or evening storms and the landscape turns lush green.
rows.highlights: Green fields, dramatic clouds and more birds around the site.
rows.tips: Carry a rain jacket or umbrella; paths can be muddy after storms — wear shoes with grip.

rows.weather: Rain tapers off, vegetation is at its most vivid and cooler mornings return.
rows.highlights: Vivid green views and softer light during the day.
rows.tips: Keep an eye on the forecast and keep your plan flexible in case a storm passes by.

seasons.note: These are long-term averages for the region, not a guarantee for any specific day or year.

In the rainy season, dramatic clouds add atmosphere — protect your equipment from sudden rain.
Respect barriers and never fly drones without prior permission.

plans.who: Much of the site can be enjoyed at ground level, but terrain is uneven and shaded rest points are limited.
points: Talk to the entrance staff about your needs — some visitors walk with canes or use a walker with care.
Focus on the main viewpoint, the interpretive area and the museum.
Bring a companion if possible; access and assistance options change often, so call ahead.

science.title: Science & Visitor Responsibility
science.subtitle: A little background on why this site matters, and the simple rules that keep it safe.
science: It was among the first great population centres of western Mesoamerica, with origins traced to around 1000 BCE and early shaft-tomb traditions.
Its conical stepped structures and raised circular plazas are unique — built with no Olmec influence and only slight links with Central Mexico.
The documented core extends over about 20 hectares, with two monumental ball courts, five outer plazas and some forty circular residential compounds around it.
Named circles such as El Guachimontón (125 m), La Iguana and El Azquelite (115 m) reveal sophisticated geometry and large-scale organisation of labour.
The Teuchitlán tradition influenced a wide region — along the Lerma river, into southern Zacatecas, the Bajío and the coastal areas of Nayarit and Colima.
respect: Stay on the marked paths and never climb, touch or lean on the structures.
Take nothing from the ground — by law, archaeological remains belong to the nation.
Respect the site rules: no entry with food, no smoking and no pets.
Ask before using drones or professional camera equipment; permits or fees may apply.
Take your rubbish out with you and keep noise low out of respect for other visitors.
